messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Thompson is a 70-year-old married man who has been working in sales for over four decades. His life took a sudden and devastating turn when he was physically assaulted outside his local grocery store late last year. The event left him with deep emotional scars that have only worsened over time. Ever since the assault, Mr. Thompson has experienced intrusive thoughts about the incident. These unwanted memories frequently resurface during quiet moments or even while he's at work. For instance, the smell of alcohol in a bar can instantly transport him back to that night outside the grocery store. He vividly recalls the attacker’s face and how the cold metal of the weapon pressed against his skin, causing him immense distress. The intensity of these intrusive thoughts has led Mr. Thompson to avoid places associated with the assault. This includes not only the grocery store where it happened but also any nearby areas that remind him of that fateful night. He numbs his feelings by retreating into a detached state, trying hard not to think about what occurred and keeping himself busy at work and home. Mr. Thompson’s sense of self has been deeply affected by this trauma. He feels unrecognizable as the person he once was; the incident has left him with an overwhelming sense that something is fundamentally wrong with him as a human being. This feeling of defectiveness is compounded by his belief that if only he had acted differently, the assault might not have happened. These negative appraisals fuel his intrusive thoughts and make it difficult for Mr. Thompson to find any relief from his distress. He often wonders why he has changed so drastically and how he can ever regain a sense of normalcy in his life. The constant cycle of self-blame and fear of encountering triggers makes him feel trapped, unable to break free from the traumatic experience. In particular, the recurring smell of alcohol reminds Mr. Thompson of the attacker’s presence that night, intensifying his anxiety and compounding his efforts to avoid any such reminders. He has come to believe that going near the scene of the assault would only exacerbate these feelings of inadequacy and self-blame. Consequently, he avoids not just the grocery store but also similar locations where alcohol might be present. The distressing thoughts and avoidance behaviors have begun to impact his work as a salesperson. He has become less engaged in social interactions at client meetings, fearing that any small trigger could send him spiraling back into memories of the assault. This has strained relationships with colleagues and clients alike, leaving him feeling isolated both professionally and personally. Mr. Thompson’s marriage has also suffered as he withdraws emotionally from his wife. She notices that he is less involved in family activities and often preoccupied by thoughts of the past. The emotional distance between them grows each day, adding to Mr. Thompson's sense of isolation and self-doubt. Despite his efforts to manage these overwhelming feelings on his own, the constant reminders and negative self-assessments have become too much for him to bear alone. What finally brought Mr. Thompson to seek help was a recent encounter at a social event where the smell of alcohol triggered a severe panic attack. In that moment, he realized that he could no longer continue living in this state of fear and disconnection. Mr. Thompson hopes that with professional support, he can begin to reclaim his sense of self and find ways to cope with his intrusive thoughts without feeling controlled by them. He is most afraid of losing the person he once was entirely but is also deeply hopeful for a future where he can navigate life’s challenges with greater peace and resilience.
